records.why: The unit storyline described a different lesson sequence from the one actually taught (for example it put a virtual lab in Lesson 3, the four structural types in Lesson 4, a diamond/graphite deep dive and community project in Lesson 7, and ball-and-stick models in Lesson 8). records.value:
Lesson 1 — PREDICT: The Three Kitchen Mysteries (40 minutes)
Learners write predictions, then watch a conductivity demonstration of aluminium wire, dry salt, salt solution and a graphite rod. The class builds the first Driving Question Board (DQB) from its own questions, and each learner draws an initial particle model. The lesson ends on the question: what is inside each solid?

Lesson 2 — PREDICT: Predicting the Invisible (80 minutes)
Learners recall valence electrons and electron arrangement from Sub-Strand 2.1, write particle-level reasons for the Lesson 1 conductivity results and predictions for melting point and strength, and post predictions and questions on the DQB. The lesson ends on the question: what happens to the electrons when sodium meets chlorine?

Lesson 3 — OBSERVE & EXPLAIN: Ionic Bonding (80 minutes)
Learners test dry salt, distilled water and salt solution, draw dot-and-cross diagrams for NaCl and MgO, write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning explanation, and build a 2-D ionic lattice from two-coloured grains to explain brittleness. The DQB gains a red question: how can graphite conduct when it has no ions?

Lesson 4 — EXPLAIN: Dot-and-Cross Diagrams and the Six Bond Types (80 minutes)
Learners sketch what they think holds the particles together in salt, aluminium and graphite, practise dot-and-cross diagrams for ionic and covalent bonding, meet all six bond types (ionic, covalent, dative covalent, hydrogen, metallic, Van der Waals) and revise their sketches into first models of each kitchen item.

Lesson 5 — OBSERVE: Practical Investigation of Physical Properties (40 minutes)
In groups, learners test the solubility, electrical conductivity and mechanical behaviour of NaCl, candle wax, graphite and aluminium, share results in a class table and link each result to bond type. New questions go on the DQB.

Lesson 6 — OBSERVE & EXPLAIN: Seeing the Invisible with Dot-and-Cross Diagrams (80 minutes)
Using a simulation (or a teacher-led projection), learners observe ionic bonding (NaCl, MgO) and covalent bonding (HCl, NH₃, CH₄), complete dot-and-cross diagrams for all five, and compare ionic transfer with covalent sharing. The DQB shows that the Lesson 4 models of aluminium and graphite still have to be tested against evidence.

Lesson 7 — EXPLAIN: Bond Types, Structures and Properties (80 minutes)
Groups mine their notebooks and a melting-point data card to write Claim-Evidence-Reasoning explanations for salt, aluminium and graphite, critique each other in a gallery walk, update the DQB and predict the properties of two new substances (iodine and iron).

Lesson 8 — MODEL BUILDING & FINAL EXPLANATION: Four Structural Types and the Complete Story (80 minutes)
Expert groups research the four structural types (giant ionic, simple molecular, giant atomic, giant metallic) and teach each other in a jigsaw. Learners write a Final Explanation paragraph, close the DQB, compare their Lesson 1 sketch with a final model, and complete a short Material-Choice Task on why aluminium and graphite suit the uses we make of them.

records.old:
Lesson 1 — PREDICT: Anchoring Phenomenon & Prior Knowledge Elicitation
Students observe the three demonstration items (salt crystal, aluminium wire, graphite rod) and record predictions about conductivity, melting point and hardness before any testing. Teacher facilitates a Predict phase: students write individual predictions, then share in pairs, then cold-call three groups to voice predictions and record them on the class Driving Question Board (DQB). Teacher introduces the driving question and activates prior knowledge of valence electrons and electron arrangement from Sub-Strand 2.1, asking: "What do you already know about how atoms share or transfer electrons?"

Lesson 2 — OBSERVE & EXPLAIN: Valence Electrons and Bond Formation
Students revisit dot-and-cross diagrams from Sub-Strand 2.1 and are guided to discuss the role of valence electrons in bond formation. Teacher demonstrates dot-and-cross diagrams for ionic bond formation (Na⁺Cl⁻) and covalent bond formation (H₂, H₂O, O₂) on the board. Learners practise drawing their own diagrams for assigned molecules in pairs. Introduction of the six bond types (ionic, covalent, dative-covalent, hydrogen, metallic, Van der Waals) with Kenyan-context examples for each. Students update the DQB with new questions arising.

Lesson 3 — OBSERVE: Virtual Lab Simulation & Dot-Cross Practice
Learners navigate online virtual laboratory simulations (or teacher-led projected simulation where devices are limited) to observe the formation of ionic and covalent bonds at the particle level. Students complete a structured worksheet drawing dot-and-cross diagrams for NaCl, MgO, HCl, NH₃ and CH₄. Pairs compare diagrams and identify patterns in electron transfer vs. sharing. Teacher cold-calls four pairs to present diagrams on the board and facilitates class correction. Students add observations to the DQB.

Lesson 4 — OBSERVE: Structures of Elements and Compounds
Teacher introduces the four structural categories: giant ionic, simple molecular, giant atomic and giant metallic. Learners use print/digital media to research the structures of NaCl (giant ionic), iodine (simple molecular), diamond and graphite (giant atomic/layered covalent) and aluminium (giant metallic). Students sketch structural diagrams in their notebooks and label the particles and forces. Small groups (4 learners) are assigned one structure each and prepare a 2-minute explanation to share with the class — jigsaw strategy.

Lesson 5 — OBSERVE: Practical Investigation of Physical Properties
Learners carry out a structured practical: testing solubility in water, electrical conductivity (simple circuit with bulb/LED), and observing relative hardness/brittleness for: NaCl (table salt), candle wax (simple molecular), graphite rod, and aluminium foil strip. Results are recorded in a class data table. Teacher facilitates whole-class data sharing and asks: "Which pattern in your data surprises you most?" — wait time 30 seconds, cold-call three students. Students connect experimental observations back to the anchoring phenomenon.

Lesson 6 — EXPLAIN: Bond Types → Physical Properties (Sensemaking)
Teacher leads structured sensemaking discussion: for each structural category, learners articulate why the bonding arrangement produces the observed physical properties (e.g., giant ionic — high melting point because many strong electrostatic attractions must be overcome; simple molecular — low melting point because only weak Van der Waals/hydrogen bonds between molecules; metallic — conducts because delocalised electrons move freely; giant atomic — very hard because every atom is covalently bonded in 3D network). Learners construct an evidence-based comparison table in their notebooks linking bond type → structure → property → everyday Kenyan example (sufuria, pencil, salt, candle wax). DQB is updated: "Which of our original questions can we now answer?"

Lesson 7 — EXPLAIN & MODEL BUILDING: Diamond, Graphite and Aluminium Deep Dive + Community Project
Learners explore the contrasting properties of diamond and graphite (both pure carbon) as a capstone explanation challenge. Teacher poses: "Same element, same type of bond — so why is one the hardest natural substance and the other slippery enough to use as a lubricant or electrode?" Groups discuss and present explanations referencing 3D tetrahedral vs. layered hexagonal structures and the presence of delocalised electrons in graphite. Learners then begin the community sensitisation project: drafting advice for a Kenyan household on the correct use and care of aluminium sufurias, graphite electrodes in torches, and NaCl in food and water treatment, grounded in bond-type reasoning.

Lesson 8 — MODEL BUILDING & DQB REVIEW: Model Revision, Project Presentation & Unit Consolidation
Learners build or refine physical ball-and-stick models of assigned molecules/structures using locally available materials (maize cobs as atoms, wire/string as bonds, clay balls colour-coded by element — echoing materials used by Kenyan primary-school teachers). Groups present their models and explain how the bonding determines at least two physical properties. Class revisits the original DQB: teacher facilitates a structured review — "Which questions did our evidence answer? What new questions remain?" Students write a final individual explanation connecting the anchoring phenomenon (salt, aluminium, graphite) back to bond types and structures. Teacher administers a short written exit task aligned to the KICD assessment rubric.

records.why: Teacher must decide what equipment the school actually has. As written, a single 1.5 V cell cannot reliably light an LED and may show almost nothing through salt solution, which would spoil the key demonstration. Checked with Ohm's law: (3 V - 1.8 V) / 100 Ω = 12 mA, a safe LED current. Please test your own tester before the lesson and use whichever bulb or LED works with your batteries.
records.old: The simple conductivity circuit uses a 1.5 V AA battery or a 4.5 V flat battery — safe for classroom use.
records.new: The simple conductivity circuit uses a low-voltage battery pack only (two 1.5 V AA cells in a holder = 3 V, or a 4.5 V flat battery) — safe for classroom use. Test the circuit before class: a single 1.5 V cell is too weak to light most LEDs (they need roughly 1.8 V or more) and may give only a very faint glow through salt solution. If you use an LED, put a resistor of about 100 Ω in series (at 3 V) so that a bare wire or the graphite rod cannot burn the LED out.

records.why: 'Atoms want electrons' is a well-known misconception (atoms do not have wishes); the real reason is that the full-shell arrangement is lower in energy. Also, 'both atoms want an electron' is replaced by the accurate idea of sharing a pair that both atoms count. Checked: Na 2,8,1 loses 1 electron to give 2,8 (neon); H needs 2 electrons for a full first shell.
records.old: Sodium has ONE valence electron. It DESPERATELY wants to get rid of it to achieve the noble gas configuration of neon. Watch what happens.' Draw the transfer arrow to Cl (2,8,7). Say: 'The electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ IS the ionic bond. Write that definition now.' 4. Move to H₂. Say: 'Hydrogen has only one valence electron. It is NOT going to transfer — both atoms want an electron.
records.new: Sodium has ONE valence electron. Losing it leaves sodium with the stable, full outer shell of neon (2,8), so the transfer is energetically favourable — atoms do not really 'want' anything, so avoid saying that. Watch what happens.' Draw the transfer arrow to Cl (2,8,7). PAUSE 10 SECONDS. Ask: 'What charge does Na now carry? Call out.' [Learners: +1.] 'Why?' WAIT 10 SECONDS. Cold-call one learner by name for the explanation. 3. Complete Na⁺Cl⁻ diagram. Say: 'The electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ IS the ionic bond. Write that definition now.' 4. Move to H₂. Say: 'Hydrogen has only one valence electron and needs one more for a full first shell. Neither atom can take the other's electron, so they SHARE a pair — both atoms count it.

records.why: Checked against the structure: in-plane C–C bonds are strong covalent bonds, while the layers are held only by weak Van der Waals forces, so a bent rod fractures along the layers instead of deforming smoothly like a metal, where layers of cations can slide while the electron sea keeps holding them together.
records.old: (c) The forces between layers are weak, so the layers slide apart easily. When a pencil is rubbed on paper, layers of graphite flake off and stay on the paper as a mark.
records.new: (c) The forces between layers are weak, so the layers slide apart easily. When a pencil is rubbed on paper, layers of graphite flake off and stay on the paper as a mark. A graphite rod cannot bend like a metal: the strong covalent bonds inside each layer are rigid and there is no sea of electrons holding layers together, so when the rod is bent it splits and snaps between the weakly held layers.
records.reference: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Liquids and Solids (network covalent solids)

value.criterion: Linking bond type and structure to properties
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly identifies ionic, metallic and layered covalent bonding for all three substances and clearly links each structure to conductivity, melting point and mechanical behaviour.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Identifies the bond type for all three substances and links most properties to structure, with one or two gaps.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Names some bond types but describes properties without linking them to structure, or mixes up the substances.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Explains conduction in terms of freely moving ions or delocalised electrons and states why they are free or fixed in each substance, including graphite and dry versus dissolved salt.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains conduction using mobile ions or electrons for most substances, but with minor omissions.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Relies on rules such as 'metals conduct' or 'ionic does not conduct' without describing particles.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Supports every claim with specific evidence from our tests and the data card (for example the bulb lighting, brittle versus bends, 660 °C and 801 °C from the data card) and clear reasoning.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives claims with some evidence from the tests, with reasoning that is sometimes incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives claims with little or no evidence, or evidence without reasoning.

value.criterion: Applying ideas to new substances and real life
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Accurately predicts the properties of iodine or iron from its structure and gives a sound Kenyan real-life reason for a material choice.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Makes a mostly correct prediction with partial justification and a simple real-life link.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Prediction is incorrect or has no reasoning, and the real-life link is missing or unclear.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Uses terms such as lattice, electrostatic, delocalised and Van der Waals precisely, and reflects clearly on how thinking changed since Lesson 1.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses most terms correctly and gives a brief reflection on how thinking changed.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Uses few scientific terms correctly and gives little or no reflection.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations), but the data contract allows only three level fields, so Below Expectations cannot be written into the printed rubric. Teachers could treat 'no attempt or work below the Approaches descriptor' as Below Expectations. Please decide whether the contract can be extended.
